Organizers said the festival begins today in New York Mills at 201 Main Street and features a flea market, raffle, outdoor grill, bake sale, Polish-merchandise vendors and beverages. Admission is free, and parking is available. Sharon Jachim, Parish Council President, Sacred Heart St. Mary Our Lady of Czestochowa, said, “Today and tomorrow, we have both the flea market and the basket raffle going on, which is an opportunity for people to find some treasures, but also, they have the opportunity to try to win a basket of their choice. There's a really big assortment of baskets to chose from. That's going on from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. Also the outdoor grill is going to be going on so people can have a snack while they're up here.” The flea market and basket raffle will run from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. today and tomorrow and from noon to 8 p.m. on Sunday. The Polish kitchen will be open only on Sunday from noon to 8 p.m. Sunday’s schedule also includes music and dancing with Tony's Polka Band starting at 1:30 p.m. and a magic show at 3 p.m. Do you have a news tip? https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/26/how-.text: Russia has long regarded Belarus as a convenient reserve for topping up its manpower in the war against Ukraine, especially after suffering heavy losses at the front.Minsk’s economic dependence, the political vulnerability of Aliaksandr Lukashenka's regime and the legal uncertainty around the Union State create conditions in which the Kremlin can act with considerable freedom.In the Belarusian corner of the internet, in recent months a large number of adverts offering Belarusians the chance to sign a contract with the Russian army, have appeared. They are circulated everywhere – in Telegram channels, in Viber chats and in local community pages where people discuss everyday issues.At times it looks almost surreal: nestled between posts about selling vegetables or finding a tutor, a sudden offer appears promising a "high salary, benefits and Russian citizenship" in return for going to war.Investigations by DW, TVNET, CityDog and Current Time have documented a sharp increase in such posts. The human rights initiative Belpol regularly highlights examples of adverts in which recruiters use Belarusian phone numbers to inspire trust.On Belpol’s Telegram channel you can see messages promising huge payouts, help with loans, "annulment of criminal convictions" and fast-track Russian citizenship.On X, the OSB Belpol account posts screenshots of ads in which Belarusians are offered a contract with a one-off payment of 4.35 million roubles and rapid issuance of a Russian passport.These examples are not isolated incidents but part of a systematic campaign targeting socially vulnerable people.What recruiters promiseBelarusians are promised the equivalent of tens of thousands of euros, high salaries, housing, food, a military pension and life insurance.Some adverts even talk about "sorting out problems with the law," which is particularly dangerous given that participation in an armed conflict abroad falls under the article on mercenary activities in Belarus' criminal code which carries a prison term of up to seven years.Recruiters insist that the service is "legal," claiming it is not mercenary activity but "service in the army of the Union State."Who signs up for a contract?Research shows that among those recruited, the majority are men from small towns and villages, people on low incomes, with debts or with existing legal problems.Many do not realise the legal consequences and some are simply looking for quick money, without understanding that they will be sent to the most dangerous sectors of the front.Human rights activists point out that foreign contract soldiers are often placed in assault units, where casualty rates are particularly high.The recruitment scheme is simple and effective. A person sees an advert on social media and writes to the recruiter, who is using a Belarusian phone number. They are then told about payments, benefits and the supposed "legality" of the service.After that they are offered rapid paperwork and travel to Russia – most often via Smolensk or Pskov. There they sign a contract and become a member of the Russian armed forces. At that point there is almost no way back.For those who agree to sign a contract, the consequences can be tragic. Beyond the risk of being killed, they face criminal liability in Belarus, possible loss of citizenship or restrictions on their rights.Many end up as "cannon fodder" in someone else’s war, which they often barely understand.Public and state responseBelarusian society has generally reacted to this with alarm.People complain about mass spam-recruitment; some turn to the Interior Ministry, but there is virtually no response.The Lukashenka regime does not officially acknowledge that recruitment is taking place, but it does nothing to stop it.Belarus is far too dependent on Russian subsidies to openly confront the Kremlin.Furthermore, mobilisation measures inside the country are being stepped up, adding extra pressure on men of conscription age.Recruitment as part of Kremlin strategyThe recruitment of Belarusians is not about random adverts or the haphazard initiative of individual actors. It is a coordinated campaign built into the Kremlin’s strategy for expanding its pool of manpower for the war against Ukraine.The legal framework of the Union State gives Moscow extra room for manoeuvre: formally, citizens of Belarus and Russia have "equal rights" and Russian institutions are trying to spin this as "equal obligations," including compulsory military service.The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warns that such an interpretation could become a basis for exerting pressure on Belarusians and attempts to mobilise them.Russia is exploiting the vulnerability of Belarusian society, its information isolation and Minsk’s political dependence in order to turn Belarus into a source of manpower.And the longer the war drags on, the more aggressive this campaign becomes.

Close Hundreds of people, mostly minors, have been arrested and dozens injured as a wave of school protests over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages spreads across France, officials say. The demonstrations began in Paris last week but have escalated to cities including Dijon, Lyon, Strasbourg, Lille and Marseille, with teenagers blockading their schools for days. The BBC's Paris correspondent Hugh Schofield is in Paris as the protests stretch into their second week. More on this story. Photograph: ITV via Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said. Photograph: ITV via Getty Images Keir Starmer Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says Kevin Rawlinson Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.32 EDT First published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10. The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already. “A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events. “First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.” Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”. He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”. View image in fullscreen Keir Starmer alongside the US president, Donald Trump, at the Nato leaders’ summit in Ankara, Turkey in July. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit. “I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before. “That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.” His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion As Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control? Read more Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility. Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence. “Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine. “Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.” Explore more on these topics Keir Starmer Europe European Union Donald Trump Foreign policy Defence policy Nato news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Donald Trump praises ‘natural businessperson’ Andy Burnham after first meeting Streeting says he began stockpiling food weeks ago amid rising threat to UK Victoria Starmer models clothes at London fashion week show Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters ‘I think he’s sensible’: constituents on Keir Starmer stepping down as MP UK defence contractors to offer 40,000 apprenticeships, placements and jobs Keir Starmer to stand down as MP to focus on world affairs Starmer says Trump wants to ‘stay in touch’ after he steps down Fund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells Healey Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
